title: Bijective Proof of Nicomachus's Theorem (OQ-00-OQ-01)
description: Provides a bijective proof of Nicomachus's theorem: 1³ + 2³ + ... + n³ = (1+2+...+n)² = T(n)². The bijection maps [k]³ = Fin k × Fin k × Fin k to a 'gnomon' in the T(n) × T(n) square. 11 theorems, 0 sorries, 0 axioms.

overview.historicalContext: Nicomachus of Gerasa (c. 100 CE) observed that 1³+2³+...+n³ = (1+2+...+n)². The bijective proof via 'staircase squares' (gnomons) was known to ancient mathematicians and provides geometric insight beyond algebraic identity.
overview.problemStatement: Give a bijective proof that the n-th cube sum equals the n-th triangular square: [1]³⊔[2]³⊔...⊔[n]³ ≅ [T(n)]².
overview.proofStrategy: The k-th gnomon in T(n)×T(n): cells at positions with T(k-1) ≤ max(row,col) < T(k). The k-th cube [k]³ = Fin k × Fin k × Fin k bijects with the k-th gnomon via an explicit construction.
keyInsights: **Gnomon decomposition**: T(k)² - T(k-1)² = k³ (algebraic identity). Each gnomon has exactly k³ cells, matching the k-th cube.
**Bijective proof**: explicit bijection Fin k × Fin k × Fin k → gnomon_k. The bijection maps (a,b,c) to a cell in the T(n)×T(n) grid.
**Staircase square**: the T(n) × T(n) square decomposes into n gnomons, each corresponding to a cube [k]³ — this is the geometric visualization.

conclusion.implications: Bijective proofs of algebraic identities reveal the combinatorial reason behind the identity, not just its algebraic truth.
openQuestions: Can the bijective proof be generalized to higher power sums?
Can the pattern Σk^p = (polynomial in T(n))^q be formally explored?
